entry.title: Fake Supreme Court website alert: SC flags “scigovinjudicial.com” as phishing domain
entry.summary:
The latest advisory follows earlier notices issued in 2023, 2025 and 2026 identifying multiple fake Supreme Court websites.

The post Fake Supreme Court website alert: SC flags “scigovinjudicial.com” as phishing domain appeared first on SCC Times.
entry.content:
The Supreme Court of India has issued another public advisory cautioning the public against fraudulent websites impersonating its official online presence. In a notice dated 3 November 2026, the Supreme Court Registry identified “scigovinjudicial.com” as a newly detected fraudulent domain that may be used to obtain sensitive personal information and confidential credentials through phishing.

[In picture: Home page of identified fake website “scigovinjudicial.com”]

The latest advisory follows earlier public notices dated 16 July 2025, 28 April 2026 and 13 August 2026, which had identified other deceptive domains created to impersonate the Supreme Court’s official website.

[In picture: Home page of original website of Supreme Court of India, “sci.gov.in”]

The Registry cautioned litigants, lawyers and other stakeholders against sharing personal or financial information through the newly identified domain, as such disclosures could facilitate data theft. It clarified that the Supreme Court’s registered official domain is sci.gov.in and advised users to verify website addresses by hovering over links before accessing them.

Previous phishing alerts issued by the Supreme Court

The Supreme Court Registry has issued a series of public notices since August 2023 to alert the public about fraudulent websites impersonating its official portal.

31 August 2023 Notice

The first notice warned against a phishing website hosted at the following URLs:

  1. http://cbins/scigv.com

  2. https://cbins.scigv.com/offence

The fraudulent page carried the heading “Offence of Money-Laundering” and sought personal details and confidential information. The Registry advised users not to disclose such information and stated that the cyber threat had been flagged to law enforcement agencies for investigation.

9 January 2025 Notice

The Registry subsequently identified 15 fraudulent domains impersonating the Supreme Court’s official website:

  1. www.scigoin.com

  2. www.scicbiovven.com

  3. www.scigoinvon.com

  4. www.scin.in

  5. www.scibovven.com

  6. www.cbisciingov.com

  7. www.judiciarycheck.in

  8. www.scis.scigovss.net

  9. www.slcmain.in

  10. www.judicialsearchinia.com

  11. www.sclm.in

  12. www.govt.judicialauthority.com

  13. www.thescoi.com

  14. www.sclcase.com

  15. www.lx-yindu.top

The Registry warned that these websites could be used to solicit personal details and confidential information and reiterated that the Supreme Court would never seek personal information, financial details or other confidential information through such websites.

16 July 2025 Notice

The next notice identified 16 fraudulent domains. It repeated the 15 domains listed in the January 2025 notice and added “www.supremecourtofindiagov.com”.

28 April 2026 Notice

The Registry identified another fraudulent domain, “scigovjudicial.com”.

The advisory cautioned users against disclosing personal or financial information through the website and stated that the cyber threat had been formally reported to law enforcement agencies.

13 August 2026 Notice

The Registry identified a further fraudulent domain, “sp-court-in.com”.

The notice again warned that the website could be used to obtain sensitive personal data and confidential credentials.

Supreme Court advises users to secure their accounts

The notice cautioned users against divulging personal or financial information through the domain. The Registry has further advised individuals who suspect that they have been compromised through the latest phishing attempt to immediately update the passwords for all their online accounts and notify their respective banks about any unauthorised access.

The Registry has also reiterated the importance of verifying electronic communications and website addresses before engaging with them. The official registered domain of the Supreme Court of India is “sci.gov.in”.

The post Fake Supreme Court website alert: SC flags “scigovinjudicial.com” as phishing domain appeared first on SCC Times.

entry.title: Call for Registrations: ‘Mediation Council of India — Lessons from the International Mediation Institute’ by Ivana Ninčić Österle
entry.summary:
The session, featuring Ivana Ninčić Österle, Executive Director of the International Mediation Institute (IMI) , will explore lessons from the International Mediation Institute in the context of the Mediation Council of India. The online session is scheduled for 24 November 2026 and is free to attend. Registrations are now open.

The post Call for Registrations: ‘Mediation Council of India — Lessons from the International Mediation Institute’ by Ivana Ninčić Österle appeared first on SCC Times.
entry.content:
About the Organiser

Sama is India’s leading Online Dispute Resolution (ODR) institution, enabling mediation, arbitration, and conciliation entirely online for businesses, government bodies, and individuals.

Since 2019, Sama has facilitated the filing of over 2.5 crore disputes and the resolution of more than 55 lakh cases, working with a panel of over 3,000 empanelled mediators, arbitrators, and case managers across 500+ districts in the country.

About the Session

Sama is hosting a virtual session with Ivana Ninčić Österle, Executive Director of the International Mediation Institute (IMI), The Hague.

India has set up its Mediation Council. Notified on 27 August 2026 under the Mediation Act, 2023, it is mandated to register mediators, set standards for their certification and ethics, and promote mediation.

IMI is based in The Hague, and was established in 2007 to set internationally applicable quality standards for mediators and an international mediator credentialing scheme, and it continues to work with mediator credentialing institutions around the world.

The session brings these two together. Ivana will share what the Mediation Council of India can take away from IMI’s experience of setting standards and credentialing mediators across jurisdictions.

For mediators, institutions, and law students, it is a chance to hear how standards, certification and ethics are approached internationally, as India’s Council takes shape.

About the Speaker

Ivana Ninčić Österle is the Executive Director of the International Mediation Institute (IMI).

A lawyer, mediator and public policy consultant for judicial reform, she specialises in mediation and judicial efficiency.

Since 2013 she has supported Serbia’s Ministry of Justice in EU integration, working on a more sustainable mediation system and leading the initiative to sign the Singapore Convention. From 2014 to 2020 she served as a national correspondent and deputy member of the European Commission for the Efficiency of Justice (CEPEJ) of the Council of Europe. She has been a registered mediator since 2016, with a practice in property, cross-border contracts and family disputes.

Who Should Attend?

This session is open to all and especially relevant for:

  • Mediation institutions and service providers

  • Bureaucrats and government officials working on mediation and justice policy

  • Lawyers and in-house legal teams

  • Mediators and other neutrals

  • Case managers

  • Law students, young lawyers and academics interested in mediation and ADR

Location

Online (Zoom)

Registration Procedure

Interested participants can register via the link mentioned at the end of this post.

Note: The joining details will be shared with registered participants on their email. Please check the spam folder if you haven’t received a confirmation email within 5 minutes of registration.

Fee

There is no registration fee. The session is free to attend.

Date and Time

Tuesday, November 24, 2026, 5:30 PM – 6:30 PM IST

Contact Information

Aditya Aryan: Aditya@sama.live

Click here to register.

entry.title: Quackery and right to health under Article 21: Allahabad High Court issues notice on PIL seeking AI-based doctor verification and stricter regulation of clinical establishments

category.term: National Commission for Indian System of Medicine Act 2020

entry.summary:
The PIL calls for an effective roadmap to eliminate quackery, prevent cross-disciplinary medical practice by unqualified persons and ensure that only duly qualified practitioners operate clinical establishments

The post Quackery and right to health under Article 21: Allahabad High Court issues notice on PIL seeking AI-based doctor verification and stricter regulation of clinical establishments appeared first on SCC Times.
entry.content:
Allahabad High Court: While considering a Public Interest Litigation (PIL) on quackery and right to life and health under Article 21 of the Constitution, seeking recognition of the right to protection from quacks and unqualified medical practitioners, and prohibition on the operation of unlicensed clinical establishments, as an integral component of the Right to Life and Health under Article 21 of the Constitution, the Division Bench of Rajan Roy and Manjive Shukla, JJ., issued notice to the respondents and directed that the matter be connected with a pending PIL raising overlapping issues.

The PIL, filed by Tulsa Devi Sewa Sansthan against the Union of India, State of Uttar Pradesh and other authorities, also seeks a systematic and effective roadmap to eliminate quackery, unauthorised medical practice and cross-disciplinary practice by practitioners lacking requisite qualifications.

The Court directed that the petition be connected with We the People v. State of U.P., PIL No. 8294 of 2016, and other connected matters, observing that some of the issues raised in the present petition were also canvassed therein. The opposite parties were permitted to file their responses.

Recognition of protection against quackery under Article 21

The petition seeks recognition of protection against quacks, unqualified medical practitioners and unlicensed clinical establishments as part of the Right to Health, protected as an aspect of the Right to Life under Article 21 of the Constitution.

It also seeks effective implementation of the Clinical Establishments (Registration and Regulation) Act, 2010, including proper constitution and functioning of the State Council of Clinical Establishments, Uttar Pradesh, under Section 8, and appointment of District Registering Authorities in every district under Section 10.

Integration of medical registers and AI-based verification of doctors

The petition highlights the need to update and integrate statutory registers of doctors and clinical establishments maintained under the Clinical Establishments Act, 2010, the National Medical Commission Act, 2019 and the National Commission for Indian System of Medicine Act, 2020.

It seeks to make these registers publicly accessible and digitally available so that individuals can verify the credentials of doctors, clinics, and hospitals. It also proposes the adoption of technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI) to verify the genuineness of medical practitioners, citing the QR-code-based verification system implemented in Telangana, which enables prospective patients to verify a doctor’s authenticity through their mobile phones.

The petition further seeks directions that registrations and permissions be granted only to practitioners and establishments whose names appear in the statutory registers, and only for the system of medicine in which the practitioners are qualified.

Uniform guidelines to prevent unauthorised medical practice

The petition also seeks effective handling of complaints relating to quackery and unqualified medical practice through the IGRS/Jansunwai grievance portal in accordance with prescribed norms.

It further seeks uniform guidelines throughout Uttar Pradesh to ensure that government doctors do not indulge in private practice, rather than leaving the issue to sporadic disciplinary action.

Additionally, it proposes that the constitution of an expert committee to recommend a ceiling on the number of establishments with which a doctor may be associated simultaneously.

Inter-departmental task force to eliminate quackery

The petition also seeks the constitution of an inter-departmental task force for implementation of penal and regulatory provisions aimed at outlawing quackery.

The Court issued notice to Respondent No. 8, directed the opposite parties to file their responses and connected the petition with PIL No. 8294 of 2016 and other connected matters.

The matter is next listed on 10 December 2026.

[Tulsa Devi Sewa Sansthan v. UOI, (PIL) No. – 1058 of 2026, decided on 29-10-2026]

Advocates who appeared in this case:

For the petitioner: Ishan Khanna, Aakash Prasad, Himanshu Singh

For the respondent: A.S.G.I., C.S.C., Kumar Ayush
